concept.shortExplanation: Because words live in a coordinate space, you can do arithmetic on them. Subtracting one vector from another leaves the difference between the two concepts as a direction you can then add somewhere else. The classic demonstration is king minus man plus woman, which lands near queen — the gender direction, extracted and reapplied. The arithmetic here is genuinely computed on live 384-dimensional embeddings; only the pool of candidate answers is fixed.
concept.ahaMoment: The analogy is not a lookup. There is no table anywhere that maps king to queen. You did coordinate arithmetic on numbers that were learned from raw text, and the resulting point in space happened to have queen as its nearest neighbour.

levels.title: The Classic
levels.instructions: Compute king − man + woman, then guess which word from the candidate pool is nearest to the result before revealing it. Every vector here is embedded live.
hints: Think about what man → king adds on top of 'man': a notion of royalty. Apply that same shift starting from 'woman' instead.

The direction from 'man' to 'king' encodes something like '+royalty'. Adding that direction to 'woman' should land you near the female equivalent of a king — and it does, by a wide margin over every other candidate.
Pick 'queen' — computed live, it comes out clearly closest to king − man + woman, well ahead of the next candidate (throne).

levels.title: Build the Direction
levels.instructions: Pick the three words yourself so the result lands nearest to the target word. You are searching for a direction in the embedding space that encodes the relationship — the maths runs live on whatever you type.
hints: You need a country → capital direction to add to 'france'. Reusing 'france' itself as one of your three terms is a trap: the result stays dominated by france's own vector and never quite reaches paris.

Pick a country/capital pair that is NOT France or Paris, subtract the country, and add france — that transplants the 'capital of' direction onto France without France's own vector fighting the result.
Add 'tokyo', subtract 'japan', add 'france' — computed live, that combination lands closest to 'paris' by a clear margin over every other candidate, including france itself.

levels.title: Predict the Similarity
levels.instructions: Before revealing the answer, estimate the cosine similarity between your computed result vector and the target. Scored on how close your estimate is to the real number.
hints: walking − walk + swim is a clean word-swap analogy (same grammatical shift applied to a different verb) — those tend to land very close to their target, not just 'somewhat similar'.
This kind of analogy usually scores a high cosine similarity, well above 0.7 — the swapped verb keeps almost all of the surrounding context intact.
Estimate around 0.90 — computed live, cos(result, 'swimming') comes out close to 0.90, near the top of the scale.
